newsitem.title: UK: Britain hesitates on the brink of Euro-currency.
newsitem.headline: Britain hesitates on the brink of Euro-currency.

text.p: With the clock ticking to the start of the European single currency in January 1999, neither of Britain's two main parties shows any inclination to break with what has become the country's tradition of joining European institutions late.
Britain looks set to sit on the sidelines while Germany, France and other core countries forge ahead with a single currency.

With less than six months before a general election which will end -- or extend -- an unprecedented 17 years of Conservative rule, neither of the main parties are prepared to commit themselves to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Prime Minister John Major has gone as far as he can to placate Conservative Eurosceptics opposed to European integration without actually ruling out entry, brandishing the opt-out negotiated at Maastricht and promising to decide later.
Labour leader Tony Blair has copied the government's wait-and-see line right down to the promise of a referendum if he decides to join later.

The result has been a frustrating lack of detailed discussion of what a single currency could mean for Britain and a growing fear that Britain may once again miss the boat. "OPT-OUT' OPTION SEEN AS UNTENABLE

"The "wait-and-see' option which dominates mainstream political thinking in the main parties will become increasingly untenable," John Monks, the general Secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC) told a recent meeting on EMU.
"Greater clarity will become necessary, otherwise it is possible the UK will be excluded by a sort of default from the most important economic development in Europe since the war."

With critics claiming the main effect of a single currency will be on jobs, Monks appears an unlikely champion of EMU. To see Britain's senior trade unionist arguing on the same side as business leaders and bankers makes it even more unusual.
Senior figures from both Labour and the Conservatives say privately political leaders' unwillingness to take a stand on a single currency has been a mistake which will have long-term consequences.
Leaving the floor open to strident Eurosceptics has charged the political atmosphere and encouraged anti-European sentiment.
A recent British Social Attitudes poll showed the share of people wanting closer ties with the European Union had fallen to 29 percent in 1995 from 37 percent in 1994.

Distrust of Europe has been heightened by the British tabloid newspaper's love of scare stories over Europe -- like the spurious tales of EU regulations banning square strawberries, short bananas or curved cucumbers.

Many leading politicians believe this, and other polls showing a solid core of anti-foreign and anti-European sentiment give a misleading impression of Britain's complex relationship with its continental neighbours.

Privately, they argue, a government committed to a single currency could win a referendum, just as in 1975 when there was a two-to-one majority for continued membership of the European Community despite early polls forecasting a "No' vote.
"The British people are indeed ambivalent about Europe," Robin Cook, Labour foreign affairs spokesman and himself on his party's Eurosceptic wing, told parliamentary reporters recently.
"...The British know that our place is in Europe, they have no serious intention of giving up that place, but they rarely manage to sound enthusiastic about it."

Although it has not not re-joined the Exchange Rate Mechanism currency grid and is unlikely to meet the three percent of GDP deficit target, Britain is well-placed as far as the economic criteria for single currency entry go.
Both Major and Blair see the Maastricht criteria setting out the entrance requirements for any country wanting to join a single currency as sound economic aims.
Indeed, the fear among political and business leaders in London is more that the criteria for entry will be fudged rather than that Britain will be kept out by them.

Privately senior Labour figures also believe Britain could get round the exchange rate clause -- highly controversial after Britain's humiliating exit from the ERM in 1992 -- by shadowing the Euro without actually rejoining the mechanism.

If the election is held at or near the deadline in May, as most commentators now expect, the government would have to rush a bill through parliament setting out the terms of Britain's entry and then call a referendum, all by the end of 1997.
One stumbling block could be the independence of the central bank, a crucial requirement for entry into a single currency.
But even drawing up the legislation to hand control of monetary policy over to a central banker could split an already fractious Conservative party.
Even Labour, which has already proposed giving the central bank more independence, although short of the level required for a single currency, would have problems.
Labour's main fear, however, is that its first term would be dominated by Europe, overshadowing key projects like plans for Welsh and Scottish assemblies and electoral reform.
But Labour is in no doubt that in the end, Britain is more likely to be in than to be out.
ELECTION BRINGS NO RESPITE FOR MAJOR
The election is unlikely to bring Major any respite.
Leading pro-Europeans, like former foreign secretary Douglas Hurd, are stepping down. Polls show the bulk of new Conservative candidates are heavily Eurosceptic.
For Labour, it is the opposite, with new candidates far more pro-European than the MPs they are likely to replace.
Some Labour insiders have already suggested this could give Blair a weapon to help him to his avowed aim of governing not just for one term but for two -- and beyond.

After a first term concentrating on domestic issues, Blair could plant his flag firmly in the European camp for the next election in five years time and ask for public backing to take Britain into a single currency.

With Euro coins due to be introduced as legal tender in the single currency bloc in 2002, voters would have a concrete vision of what a single currency would mean, and Blair would be able once again to divide -- and conquer -- the Conservatives, supporters say.
